source.title: Why is parameter averaging beneficial in SGD? An objective smoothing perspective
source.authors: Atsushi Nitanda; Ryuhei Kikuchi; Shugo Maeda; Denny Wu

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied, including appendices and additional experiments; no apparent truncation affecting the study.
record.tranche_reason: Reports the effect of parameter averaging and step-size schedules on test accuracy for image classifiers, extending the generalization-gap claim to this intervention and these settings. It does not test the listed claim versions directly.
record.gate_note: The study compares parameter-averaged SGD with SGD and reports test accuracies, but does not report training error alongside those accuracies or test memorization of random labels. Its toy analyses concern optimization distance to a smoothed-objective minimizer, not the claim versions. No rows are recorded for cited prior results or for the authors' reported comparison of averaged SAM with SAM.
record.test_reason: The study uses the broader flatness–generalization connection to motivate parameter averaging and reports optimization theory and its method's performance. It does not test V1–V8. In particular, its directional loss landscapes and Hessian trace do not measure V7's magnitude-scaled perturbation tolerance or its ranking of generalization gaps against other measures.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially correct. The authors establish sufficient conditions for averaged SGD to approach a smoothed-objective minimizer more closely than SGD, and recommend large learning rates with averaging for difficult datasets. Their experiments show improved held-out performance and distinct solutions; the theoretical conditions are not established for neural networks.
record.recipe_differences: Studies tail parameter averaging of SGD and SAM on image classification, rather than the listed interventions concerning memorization, width, architecture, optimizer choice, batch size, dropout, sharpness measures, or example removal.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies with dataset and step-size schedule: the authors report large-step averaging helps more on CIFAR100 than CIFAR10, and report the large-step schedule gives only small improvement on CIFAR10. Results are also presented across model architectures.

fits_no_version.finding: Tail averaging improves test accuracy in all six matched schedule-s SGD comparisons in Table 2 and all six matched cosine-s comparisons in Table 4.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Tail parameter averaging can improve CIFAR10 and CIFAR100 test accuracy across the tested CNN architectures.

fits_no_version.finding: For multi-step averaged SGD, delaying decay improves CIFAR100 accuracy, whereas Table 3's schedule l performs worse than s or m on CIFAR10. The schedule-l SGD accuracies are not tabulated.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The benefit of maintaining a large learning rate during parameter averaging depends on the dataset and schedule.

fits_no_version.finding: Figures 5 and 11 associate averaging with a flatter directional landscape or lower Hessian trace and better held-out performance, without magnitude-aware perturbation measurements.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Parameter averaging can produce flatter solutions with better held-out performance under these particular flatness measurements.

fits_no_version.finding: After 600 epochs of averaged SGD on ResNet-50/CIFAR100, another 200 epochs of small-step SGD improve training loss while worsening test loss and reducing test accuracy from 83.35% to 82.42% (Figure 6).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Further minimizing training loss from an averaged solution can worsen held-out performance.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics
record.problems: The experiments report test accuracy but not training error, so they do not directly quantify a training-test gap. Schedule-l comparisons lack matched SGD accuracy values in the displayed tables. The averaging hyperparameters were tuned based on validation performance. Main table accuracies use 5 runs for ResNet-50 and WRN-28-10, and 3 for Pyramid Network; cosine annealing table 4 reports no standard deviations.
record.rows_left_out: No reported rows were left out; 36 result rows are recorded. The 60-row limit was not reached.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and held-out performance compared with natural-label training under the same architecture and recipe.
Width sweeps beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and the contribution of local connectivity or initialization.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning; averaged SGD and SAM are not adaptive optimizers of the kind named.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that remove a large-batch penalty.
Dropout interventions, small-data regimes, and joint removal of dropout and weight decay.
Magnitude-scaled weight-perturbation tolerance, its association with training–test error gaps at similarly low training loss, and its ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: All 36 rows retain versions ["none"]; their cannot_determine states describe applicability to the listed versions, not uncertainty about the reported accuracies. These method-performance rows should not count as claim-test evidence. Correct the record's blanket assertion that training loss is unreported: Figures 5 and 6 explicitly show training and test losses, although the accuracy tables do not report training error. The rows_left_out statement is also inaccurate: Table 3's additional schedule-l results, SAM results, and Figures 5, 6 and 11 are omitted. None supplies a missing test of V1–V8.

versions.untested_parts: Natural-label versus random-label training and held-out performance.
Network-width sweep beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparisons.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under tuning conditions.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets.
Magnitude-aware sharpness measurement and comparison with other generalization measures.
Removal and retraining of memorized examples.
